subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Jonathan's Coffee House and the Stock Exchange
description: One-minute skill: Jonathan's Coffee House and the Stock Exchange.

hook.text: The London Stock Exchange began in Jonathan's Coffee House on Exchange Alley in the 1690s.

buildup.text: Stockjobbers gathered daily at Jonathan's to buy and sell shares. The owner posted ships' arrivals and price lists.

discovery.text: Jonathan's became so crowded that traders spilled onto the street, shouting trades through windows and doorways.

twist.text: In 1698, the shop was expelled for rowdy behavior. Traders simply moved next door and carried on.

climax.text: By 1801, the traders formalized into the London Stock Exchange—but the culture started over coffee.

punchline.text: Global finance was born between coffee cups on a London alley.

quiz.question: What was Jonathan's Coffee House's role in financial history?
options: It funded the Bank of England
Stock traders gathered there, eventually forming the London Stock Exchange

details.summary: Jonathan's Coffee House in London's Exchange Alley became the informal trading floor where brokers bought and sold shares in the late 1600s. Stock prices were listed on the walls. It eventually formalized into the London Stock Exchange, one of the foundations of modern capitalism.
details.whyItMatters: The birth of the London Stock Exchange in a coffeehouse illustrates how informal gathering spaces can generate institutions that drive the global economy.
takeaways: Jonathan's Coffee House hosted informal stock trading
Share prices were posted on the coffeehouse walls
It evolved into the London Stock Exchange

faq.question: When did Jonathan's Coffee House become the Stock Exchange?
faq.answer: Informal trading at Jonathan's began in the 1690s. By 1698, John Castaing published regular share price lists there. In 1773, the traders formalized the arrangement and moved to a dedicated building, officially becoming the London Stock Exchange.

faq.question: Were other financial institutions born in coffeehouses?
faq.answer: Yes. Beyond Lloyd's Insurance and the Stock Exchange, the Bank of England was discussed in coffeehouses, and auction houses like Sotheby's began nearby. London's entire financial district grew around the coffeehouse cluster in Exchange Alley.
